Lake citations list official cite 514 U.S. 1, parallel cites 115 S. Ct. 1185 and 131 L. Ed. 2d 34, and vendor-neutral cite 1995 U.S. LEXIS 1806.

defect.evidence_quote: There is no indication that the arresting officer was not acting objectively reasonably when he relied upon the police computer record. Application of the Leon framework supports a categorical exception to the exclusionary rule for clerical errors of court employees.
defect.problem: The core good-faith proposition is supported, but the holding text is truncated and should avoid implying that this record conclusively found a court clerk caused the error in this case.
defect.proposed_fix: Replace with: "The good-faith exception applies when an arresting officer reasonably relies on an erroneous warrant record attributable to clerical errors of court employees; suppression is unwarranted because exclusion would not meaningfully deter such court-clerk errors."

reasons: The opinion supports the legal rule through its categorical-exception language.

The opinion frames court-clerk responsibility conditionally: "If court employees were responsible" and "If it were indeed a court clerk," because the trial court made no factual finding on whether the Justice Court or Sheriff's Office caused the stale record.
residual_risks: The disclosed content_page holding ends with a dangling "here, a…" fragment.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: State the rule conditionally for errors attributable to court employees and remove the incomplete parenthetical.

reasons: The opinion expressly applies Leon's good-faith framework to a new setting involving erroneous warrant records and court-employee clerical errors.

The opinion states that application of the Leon framework supports a categorical exception to the exclusionary rule for clerical errors of court employees, which supports the home role as Good-Faith Exception progeny/refinement.
residual_risks: The word Key is an editorial importance label, but the disclosed SCOTUS opinion and categorical-exception holding support treating the case as central rather than incidental.
